rv.q: If you want to be deeply, profoundly disturbed by a night at the theatre, there's no finer way to do it than this.
What a play. What a production.
Sensational turns from Anderson and Billy Crudup are made even better by the ultra-intimate staging at @sohoplace.
This interminable verbal slugfest is a love-hate affair for the audience, as well as Martha and George.
This is one of the big-news shows of 2026, a production I bet will eventually make it over to Broadway.
Vicious repartee absolutely crackles
This is a chance to see two actors at the top of their game, and at exhaustive, almost exhausting length.
Marianne Elliott’s revival is emphatically that: very vicious, very funny, pulling and punching with the rhythm of a comedy.

Anderson and Crudup can hold their own against that landmark adaptation of the play about George, a middle-aged history professor with a sagging academic libido, and Martha, his frustrated, ceaselessly needling wife.
There’s so much to admire here, but too little range.
There’s no better after party in the West End right now than Marianne Elliott’s production of Edward Albee’s American classic Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?
It is a great night at the theatre.
Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? is stylish, acerbic and dramatic; an entertaining, emotional rollercoaster delivered by a brilliant cast.
No need to confess that this is an exhilarating evening, despite some mild reservations.
Crudup and Anderson have a tight grip on each undulation, never over-peppering the seething anger, never underplaying their nearly forgotten attraction.
Strong performances from a cast able to stamp their own authority on well-known characters made for a very satisfying night out.
A feast of caustic barbs delivered with wry humour and sexual tension, this production takes a gentler approach to the internecine excoriation inherent in Albee’s text.
As brutal as it is funny, you leave this production bruised by its brutality and thrilled by its wit and intelligence.
This is theatre of the highest calibre: intelligent, exhilarating and emotionally shattering.
Now Marianne Elliott has revived it with thrilling success at @sohoplace featuring brilliant leading performances from its two American stars Gillian Anderson and Billy Crudup.

Marianne Elliott's rich and propulsive new production of Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf @sohoplace skillfully avoids the quicksand, ensuring the audience live through the wreckage alongside the characters as we're all invited to an afterparty with Martha and George.
For me, this is one of the most entertaining shows in London right now.
Instead it grips and captivates with stellar acting performances that never cease in their uncomfortable tension and humorous wit.

It is, admittedly, a little exhausting watching the pair cut lumps out of each other and it hits a lull during the lengthier second half that combines acts two and three with a brief pause between them.
Carried by Albee’s brilliant dialogue, the play is always riveting.
The fact that the characters continue to live in my imagination after the curtain falls is perhaps enough to prove just how vividly alive this production feels.

The audience is both onlooker and palpably immersed in their sniping. Set on a 1960s university campus, Martha (Gillian Anderson) and her history professor husband George (Billy Crudup) arrive home drunk in the early hours.
Giving this confessional drama their all this time it’s superstars Gillian Anderson and Billy Crudup, in a terrific revival directed by Marianne Elliott.
What truly impresses about this production is how it uses the intimacy to increase the intensity, making for a raw and often uncomfortable watch.
This strong revival of the classic play is made especially effective by the intimacy of @sohoplace.
It’s a baffling 3 hours and 20 minutes in the theatre, and I am afraid to say there are better ways to spend that time.
If you are willing to invest the time, who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf will reward you with excellent performances, psychological intensity, dark humour, and a script that positively fizzes.
This is engrossing, thrilling theatre.
An absolute tour de force, Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf is an overwhelming display of craftsmanship that delivers nothing but theatre at its best.
This three-and-a-half-hour slinging match is sublime.
It’s a total theatrical privilege to be in such an intimate venue as @sohoplace, which leaves nowhere for the actors, the characters or the audience to hide.

cn.t: Critics hail Anderson and Crudup's electrifying performances in Elliott's intimate revival, praising the production's crackling intensity and dark humor. A few find the three-hour runtime exhausting or the staging too light, but most call it unmissable theater.
